title: ‘Pretty low’: Calgary girls' hockey team out $2,000 after tournament scam
summary: A Calgary U-11 girls' hockey team lost nearly $2,000 — and the opportunity to play a tournament they thought they were accepted to — after falling victim to a scam. Last month, Hockey Alberta issued…

image.caption: Coach Dave Wilder says the team will add more checks and balances after falling victim to a tournament scam. (Submitted by Dave Wilder)

blocks.text: Calgary

A Calgary U-11 girls' hockey team lost nearly $2,000 — and the opportunity to play a tournament they thought they were accepted to — after falling victim to a scam. Last month, Hockey Alberta issued a warning on social media that it’s seeing a growing number of spoofed emails requesting money for tournaments.
Hockey Alberta warned last month it's seeing more of these scams
A Calgary U-11 girls’ hockey team lost nearly $2,000 — and the opportunity to play a tournament they thought they were accepted to — after falling victim to a scam.
Coach Dave Wilder says team volunteers applied to a tournament listed on Hockey Alberta's website slated to be held in Red Deer, Alta., in February.

They got an email saying they were admitted to the tournament, though it came from a different email address than the one listed on Hockey Alberta's website. At the time, Wilder says they didn’t think too much of it — teams and tournaments regularly create specific email addresses.
The email asked for $1,950, which they paid. It was only when they got another email asking for a deposit of $900 that the team got suspicious and started digging into it further.

That’s when they found out the girls actually hadn’t been accepted to the tournament, and scammers had made off with the money. The team filed a police report and is waiting to hear back if Scotiabank will reimburse them.
“Stealing money from little kids is a pretty low low,” Wilder said. “I'm not sure how it'll work out in the future, but there will definitely be more steps of due diligence involved.”
Scams on the rise

Last month, Hockey Alberta issued a warning on social media that it’s seeing a growing number of spoofed emails requesting money for tournaments. Teams across the country have posted similar warnings.
The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre calls it spear phishing, and says it’s on the rise.

“In these types of fraud, criminals often take the time to research their intended targets,” the centre said in a statement, using social media, tournament schedules and hockey association websites to their advantage.

“Fraudsters understand that hockey teams regularly register for tournaments, pay registration fees and operate under deadlines. They take advantage of these routine activities, established relationships and the trust that exists within these communities.”

There were $87 million in losses from spear phishing in the first nine months of this year, a nearly 28-per-cent increase compared to all of 2025, the centre said. It also believes many frauds go unreported.
To protect themselves, the fraud centre recommends teams independently verify all payment requests and contact tournament owners directly.
Going forward

As for why more scammers might be targeting hockey teams, Wilder says it could be a case of supply and demand. Ice time is limited, as is tournament space, and scammers likely know teams might be eager to jump on any opportunity.
“I don't know if I'll let any of this ever slip through my hands again. I might have to drive to Red Deer to verify these people exist,” said Wilder.
The team has told parents about the scam, but so far not the girls. Wilder’s not sure they’ll be able to find another tournament to play in, and might instead schedule some exhibition games.
Parents were frustrated, he said, but still willing to pitch in. The team plans to find ways to fundraise to make up the missing funds.
